questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Two-Dimensional Vector in a Different Basis
questions.problem: Let $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}},$ where ${b}_{1}=2{c}_{2}$ and ${b}_{2}=-5{c}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]$, we can write $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-3{c}_{1}+5{c}_{2} \\  & =5{c}_{2}-3{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(2{c}_{2})-\frac{3}{5}(5{c}_{1}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{b}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}].$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3{b}_{1}-6{b}_{2} \\  & =-6{b}_{2}+3{b}_{1} \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}(5{b}_{2})-\frac{3}{2}(-2{b}_{1}) \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}{c}_{1}-\frac{3}{2}{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{6}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={c}_{1}-2{c}_{2} \\  & =-2{c}_{2}+{c}_{1} \\  & =2(-{c}_{2})+\frac{1}{3}(3{c}_{1}) \\  & =2{b}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{b}_{2}\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}},$ where ${c}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}{b}_{3}$, ${c}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}{b}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we can write $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}-{b}_{3} \\  & =-{b}_{3}+2{b}_{2}+5{b}_{1} \\  & =5(-\frac{1}{5}{b}_{3})+2\cdot 2(\frac{1}{2}{b}_{2})+5\cdot 2(\frac{1}{2}{b}_{1}) \\  & =5{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}+10{c}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4 \\ 10\end{aligned}].$

questions.worked_solution:
Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]$, we can write $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-3{b}_{2}+6{b}_{3} \\  & =-3{b}_{2}+6{b}_{3}+{b}_{1} \\  & =3(-{b}_{2})+3(2{b}_{3})+{b}_{1} \\  & =3{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -7\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}=4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. From the second equation, we get 

$$
{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=4(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})+{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}={c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -7\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-7{b}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}-7({c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}-7{c}_{1}+14{c}_{2} \\  & =-7{c}_{1}+\frac{29}{2}{c}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ \frac{29}{2}\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}=2{b}_{2}-{b}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}=3{b}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=2{b}_{2}-{b}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}=3{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. From the second equation, we get 

$$
{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=2{b}_{2}-(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2})\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{6}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{b}_{1}+8{b}_{2} \\  & =5(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2})+8(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{6}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{c}_{2}+4{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{c}_{2} \\  & =4{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}={b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}={b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. Multiplying the second equation by $-1$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=-{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}={c}_{2}-{c}_{1}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}+({c}_{2}-{c}_{1})\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\  & =2(2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})+({c}_{2}-{c}_{1}) \\  & =4{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}+{c}_{2}-{c}_{1} \\  & =3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}=-4{b}_{1}+5{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=-4{b}_{1}+5{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. Multiplying the second equation by $5$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}+5{c}_{2}=6{b}_{1}\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{c}_{1}+\frac{5}{6}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=-4(\frac{1}{6}{c}_{1}+\frac{5}{6}{c}_{2})+5{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=\frac{2}{6}{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{6}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3{b}_{1}-6{b}_{2} \\  & =3(\frac{1}{6}{c}_{1}+\frac{5}{6}{c}_{2})-6(\frac{2}{6}{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{6}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{c}_{1}-\frac{3}{2}{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}},$ where ${c}_{1}=2{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}={b}_{1}-{b}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=2{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{1}-{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. Adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=3{b}_{1}\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=2(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2})+{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6{b}_{1}-{b}_{2} \\  & =6(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2})-(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2}) \\  & =2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{8}{3}{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3} \\ \frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}].$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065354/assets/aed9216ce4c536aad07f26eec0e0cb7e3032147a19c13e0a2d42925083c49518.png) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_2-\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = 2\mathbf{b}_1 - 3\mathbf{b}_2?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}-3{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
2\mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{b}_2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\mathbf{c}_1 = \left( -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2 \right) - \mathbf{b}_1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_1 = -3\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.
$$

Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065354/assets/80531bde3f2ebb6314a3a297efa44e3e21a33d0b5f628c67c39ef0fa288f4c78.png) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1$ and $\mathbf c_2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-3{b}_{2} \\  & =(-3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})-3(-2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}) \\  & =-3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}+6{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2} \\  & =3{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065354/assets/f678c1ecc9878c30b04e891af9e6933f1edb42af8e155c3f4719838210e1cc1d.png)
